seo.title: Karmic tail 6 11 14 compatibility: the couple's tail explained
seo.description: Karmic tail 6 11 14 compatibility: The Lovers, Strength and Temperance. Why a couple has Strength where Judgement should stand, and who tames whom.

title: The 6-11-14 karmic tail in compatibility: a taming with no winner
short: The couple's karmic tail 6-11-14 — The Lovers, Strength and Temperance — holds an oddity that only the numbers reveal. For a single person, the road from The Lovers to Temperance always runs through Judgement: 6 + 14 = 20. For a couple, that place is taken by Strength, 11. Where one person alone would face a verdict from outside, two people are left alone with each other, and they start taming each other.

sections.h2: The first clue: Strength where Judgement should stand
paragraphs: A couple's tail is counted differently from a personal one. Each of its three points is the sum of the same points of two personal matrices, reduced to 22. So the middle of a couple's tail is not derived from its two ends, as it is for one person; it is assembled from the middles of two personal tails. By the personal formula this place would hold Judgement: a personal 6-20-14 tail does exist. A personal 6-11-14 tail does not exist at all — only two people can add it up.
Running through every date since 1900 shows how couples assemble their Strength:

ul: **20 + 9 → 11** — in 45% of couples: one partner has Judgement in the middle of the personal tail, the other has The Hermit;
**5 + 6 = 11** — in 30%: one partner's Hierophant and the other's Lovers;
**19 + 19 → 11** — in 22%: both have The Sun in the middle, and their personal tails are identical, 12-19-7;
the remaining 3% — the combinations 19 + 10 and 20 + 18.

paragraphs: In almost half of these couples (46%), Judgement has not gone anywhere: one of the two carries it in their personal matrix. But added to the other partner's card, it stops being Judgement and becomes Strength. One person's verdict turns into the strength of two — or into a struggle between two, depending on how they use it.

The second clue is stricter still. In these couples, neither partner has Strength or Temperance in their personal tail — not in any of the five combinations. The Lovers appear in one partner's personal tail in 30% of couples, and in 70% of couples none of the three cards appears in either personal tail. Nobody brings the middle or the main task of this tail with them: these cards appear only between the two.

The ends of the tail, meanwhile, behave just as they would for one person: the entry equals the main task plus the centre. With The Sun at the centre, 14 + 19 = 33 → 6; with The Wheel of Fortune, 14 + 10 = 24 → 6. Only the middle breaks the rule — the very point where a single person would have Judgement.

And one coincidence is too exact to pass over. In The Taming of the Shrew a servant describes a "taming-school" whose master is Petruchio, teaching "tricks eleven and twenty long". The phrase alludes to the card game thirty-one: 11 + 20 = 31, meaning "exactly right". Eleven and twenty are the very two cards that compete for the middle of this tail. Shakespeare knew nothing of the destiny matrix, of course, but his master of taming counts in exactly these numbers.

Shakespeare wrote The Taming of the Shrew in the early 1590s. Some twenty years later John Fletcher — Shakespeare's co-author on his late plays and his successor as chief playwright of the King's Men — wrote a sequel: The Woman's Prize, or The Tamer Tamed. Katherina is dead by now, Petruchio marries Maria, and on the very first night Maria shuts herself up in the house with her allies and sets her husband terms.

In November 1633 the two plays were performed one after the other before Charles I and Queen Henrietta Maria at St James's Palace: Shakespeare's on Tuesday the 26th, Fletcher's on Thursday the 28th. The Master of the Revels, Sir Henry Herbert, noted that the first was "liked" and the second "very well liked". In a single week the king and queen saw both ends of one story.

Shakespeare's play has a frame that is often forgotten. A drunken tinker, Christopher Sly, is picked up outside an alehouse, carried to a lord's bed and assured that he is a lord. The play is performed for him, and as a remedy: "Seeing too much sadness hath congeal'd your blood, / And melancholy is the nurse of frenzy, / Therefore they thought it good you hear a play". Fletcher's prologue repeats the prescription: if you fall sick of melancholy, "see't agen. / 'Tis no dear Physick". Both plays about a couple present themselves as a way to restore measure.

In the anonymous 1594 play The Taming of a Shrew, a close relative of Shakespeare's, the frame closes. Sly wakes outside the alehouse and announces, "I know now how to tame a shrew" — and sets off home to try it on his wife. The recipe for taming turns out to be a drunken tinker's dream. This is worth keeping in mind: everything that follows between Petruchio and Katherina is a dream that another person can be remade, and the play itself warns that it is a dream.

The cards of the tail fall onto the two plays in order. The wooing and the first sparring match are The Lovers. Shakespeare's taming and Fletcher's counter-taming are Strength. Fletcher's epilogue is Temperance.

sections.h2: Entry to the task: The Lovers, whose common language is sparring
paragraphs: The entry to the task is what the couple wants together, its agreements and its common language. On the couple's chart it is the same point as "Common language" on the relationship line. Katherina and Petruchio find their common language with the first line they exchange, and it is the language of sparring. A minute after meeting, they are already finishing each other's puns:
— Who knows not where a wasp does / wear his sting? In his tail. / — In his tongue.

The sting of these two really is in the tongue. Her sister's suitors are afraid of Katherina, her father is worn out by her, her music teacher left with a lute broken over his head. Petruchio is the first to answer her at her own speed. That is The Lovers at the entry: attraction to a person with whom there is no need to pretend. Waite calls this card simply "in all simplicity the card of human love".

But the entry stands on the line of tasks, and the same wish turns into resistance. Shakespeare shows where Katherina's shrewishness comes from before the wooing even begins: her sister is loved, and she is not. "She is your treasure, she must have a husband; / I must dance bare-foot on her wedding day," she throws at her father. When Petruchio comes to woo, her father tells him the main thing is to win her love, "for that is all in all". Petruchio replies: "Why, that is nothing." At the entry the two want the same thing — a love in which you are the one chosen — and at once argue over whether it is needed at all.

For Wen, The Lovers is above all a card of choice, and this wooing is exactly where the choice is missing. The father and the suitor settle the dowry without the bride. "Will you, nill you, I will marry you," says Petruchio — willing or not. Consent is skipped in the very first scene. Katherina will say her "yes" not at the altar but much later — on the road and in the middle of a street.

In the life of a couple with this tail, the entry is easy to recognise. The two find a tone only they understand: teasing, arguing for the sake of it, flirting through challenge. Others think they are quarrelling; they think they are talking. The trouble starts when tenderness can no longer be heard in this language and only the score of jabs is left. Lisovskaya describes the minus of The Lovers in a couple as a swing of "peace, then war", words that wound more than intended, and jealousy that grows out of self-doubt. Such a couple can be loud in public too. At the wedding Petruchio swears so loudly that the priest drops his book, and when he stoops to pick it up, the groom cuffs him; the whole church hears the kiss.

sections.h2: Middle of the task: Strength, or the taming-school
paragraphs: In Lisovskaya's book the middle of a couple's tail has no meaning of its own: it is an addition to the main task. We read it as the road — what the couple does and goes through on its way from the wish to the task. For these two, the road runs through Strength.

Shakespeare names it outright: "For I am he am born to tame you Kate, / And bring you from a wild Kate to a Kate / Conformable as other household Kates." The pun in the original rests on the name: Kate sounds like cat, and Petruchio promises to turn a "wild Kate" into a "household" one.

He describes his method as a falconer would: "My falcon now is sharp and passing empty… Another way I have to man my haggard… That is, to watch her, as we watch these kites". The meat is "burnt", the bed is badly made, and all of it is done "in reverend care of her". A servant sums it up in one line: "He kills her in her own humour." Another does the arithmetic more precisely: "By this reckoning he is more shrew than she." Petruchio wins by becoming more of a shrew than the shrew.

This is the first trap of Strength in a couple: the two compete over who can hold out longer. Petruchio explained the arithmetic himself before the wedding: "And where two raging fires meet together / They do consume the thing that feeds their fury". Two fires are an exact picture of the middle 11 in every fifth couple with this tail, where it is made of one partner's Sun and the other's.

Wen writes about Strength what Petruchio missed: a person "cannot use brute force to exercise will over others" and must use "gentle, subtle influence". For her, Strength is mastery of the self, while The Chariot is mastery of the world around. Lisovskaya describes the minus of Strength in a couple as a competition: each wants to be in charge, each has their own truth, and the other's view is not accepted. In the plus is what the play reaches only in its fifth act: one partner accepts the other's lead, flexibility appears, and tension turns into passion.

In daily life the middle 11 shows itself in small things that decide whose word is last: who picks the road, who decides whether the food is "all right", who falls silent first and stays silent longer. Pressure rarely looks like an order. More often it looks like care that leaves the other no choice. Shakespeare's Petruchio is the extreme case: hunger and sleeplessness. In a real couple this is not the task of the tail but a boundary. If one partner holds the other through fear, by withholding food, sleep, money or contact, or through threats, outside help is needed: a psychologist, a crisis line, and in danger — a local emergency number.

paragraphs.h3: The tamer who had been tamed before

paragraphs: Fletcher saw in Shakespeare's play what Shakespeare had left offstage: Strength works both ways. In the very first scene of the sequel, friends recall the late Katherina: she "turn'd his temper, / And forc'd him blow as high as she"; the bare remembrance of her "will make him start in's sleep". Petruchio himself calls that taming "my twelve strong labours to reclaim her, / Which would have made Don Hercules horn mad, / And hid him in his Hide". Hercules' hide, as everyone knows, was a lion's. The tamer came out of his first marriage tamed and never noticed.

Maria answers Petruchio in his own language. In Shakespeare he trained a "haggard", a wild hawk caught full-grown. Maria declares: "I am no more the gentle, tame Maria… I have a new soul in me / Made of a North wind, nothing but tempest" — and praises the free haggard, "that woman, that hath wing, and knows it". Her means are the same as his: refusal, siege, a bet on who will hold out longer. Across two plays one and the same man was both the tamer and the tamed. The role in the middle of this tail is tied neither to sex nor to character: it passes from hand to hand.

paragraphs.h3: A Judgement staged in a coffin

paragraphs: Then Fletcher stages a Judgement — the very card that is missing from the middle of the couple's tail. Petruchio pretends to be dead and is carried in in a coffin. Over the coffin Maria pronounces her verdict: she weeps not for him but for his life — "His poor unmanly, wretched, foolish life". The dead man cannot bear it, rises, and a few lines later says, "I am born again."

The scene is funny, but the mechanism is serious. When two people lack honest Strength, they stage a Judgement for themselves: a loud scene with a verdict and a resurrection, after which everything seems to start with a clean slate. In a comedy it works. In a couple such a scene brings relief but not measure: the score has not been reset; only the winner has changed.

sections.h2: The couple's atmosphere: an argument about the sun
paragraphs: The centre of the couple's chart is the atmosphere — what happens between the two when nobody is watching. In 77% of couples with the 6-11-14 tail the centre is The Sun; in 23% it is The Wheel of Fortune. No date ever puts The Sun at the centre of a personal chart: only two people can light it. Most often it comes from centres 9 and 10 (The Hermit and The Wheel, 45% of couples) or 7 and 12 (The Chariot and The Hanged Man, 30%).

The most famous scene of The Taming of the Shrew is the argument about the sun. Petruchio and Katherina are riding to her father's, it is broad day, and Petruchio says: "Good Lord, how bright and goodly shines the moon!" She objects: it is the sun. He orders the horses turned back. And then Katherina answers in a way that can be heard in two ways:

Then, God be bless'd, it is the blessed sun: / But sun it is not, when you say it is not; / And the moon changes even as your mind. / What you will have it named, even that it is; / And so it shall be so for Katharina.

This is The Sun at the centre of the couple in both of its forms at once. In the minus, one partner decides what counts as the sun, and the atmosphere rests on the other agreeing; Lisovskaya names total control and attempts to restrict the partner among the minuses of The Sun. The plus begins a minute later. An old man comes towards them, Petruchio greets him as a fair young maid, and Katherina takes up the game with such zest that the old man calls her "my merry mistress". Then she "apologises": her eyes, she says, "have been so bedazzled with the sun / That everything I look on seemeth green". For the first time the two laugh not at each other but together. Waite's list of meanings for The Sun includes "fortunate marriage". In the play this sun rises at the very moment the argument becomes a shared game.

Right after this scene comes the kiss in the street. "First kiss me, Kate, and we will." — "What, in the midst of the street?" — "What, art thou ashamed of me?" — "No, sir, God forbid; but ashamed to kiss." He threatens to turn for home, and she kisses him: "Nay, I will give thee a kiss: now pray thee, love, stay." Here, for the first time, she calls him "love". The entry of the tail, The Lovers, is fulfilled in public, without the father and without the dowry.

paragraphs.h3: When the Wheel of Fortune is at the centre

paragraphs: In 23% of couples the centre is The Wheel. Then the couple's atmosphere is a game of chance and a wager. In the last scene of the Shrew the husbands bet on whose wife is the most obedient, and the widow teases Petruchio with a proverb: "He that is giddy thinks the world turns round." Lisovskaya sees in a couple's Wheel an alternation of rises and crises and advises not to fight the alternation itself. Such a couple will easily recognise itself in Cole Porter's musical Kiss Me, Kate (1948): divorced actors play Petruchio and Katherina and, in the course of the show, live through their own story a second time.

sections.h2: Main task: Temperance, or two drops of equal weight
paragraphs: The main point of the tail is Temperance. It is read mostly through its minus: what the couple cannot manage and what it has to learn. For all their differences, both plays end in the same minus, the one Lisovskaya describes for a couple with Temperance: one partner keeps giving way, and the other never even thinks of it.

In Shakespeare this is Katherina's famous speech. Three husbands bet a hundred crowns on whose wife will come at the first call. Only Katherina comes, and she lectures the headstrong wives on duty: "But now I see our lances are but straws, / Our strength as weak, our weakness past compare, / That seeming to be most which we indeed least are." Two cards of the tail meet in one speech. Strength is declared an illusion, and measure — lower your pride, she tells the wives — is demanded of one side only.

Whether this is meant seriously or ironically has been argued for four hundred years. The last line of the play leaves the question open: "'Tis a wonder, by your leave, she will be tamed so." She will be tamed — that is, she lets herself be. The taming Petruchio dreamed of as his victory rests on her consent.

In Fletcher the score is reversed. Over the coffin Maria has got her way, and at once she says: "From this hour make me what you please: I have tam'd ye, / And now am vow'd your servant… Dare you kiss me? / Thus I begin my new love." Again one side gives everything away — only now it is the other one. And again the play ends with a kiss and a new love: the tail returns to its entry, to The Lovers.

In daily life the minus of Temperance looks ordinary. The same partner always apologises. Peace in the house rests on the other keeping quiet. A quarrel is not taken to a real conversation but put out by surrender, and resentment piles up until one day the score flips, as it does in Fletcher. Among the tasks of Temperance in a couple Lisovskaya names lost balance, suppressed feelings, haste and the wish to control the partner — and all of them can be seen in these two marriages.
Fletcher put the answer to the main task into Maria's mouth earlier, when Petruchio demands "due obedience" from her:
Take two small drops of water, equal weigh'd, / Tell me which is the heaviest, and which ought / First to descend in duty?

The question is not who is right but who gives way. Two drops of equal weight are two people, neither of them heavier. And Petruchio takes his first step towards measure in reply: "I urge not service from you, nor obedience / In way of duty, but of love, and Credit".
The play's epilogue reads like a formula for the main task, one a couple could write about itself:

The Tamer's tam'd, but so, as nor the men / Can find one just cause to complain of, when / They fitly do consider in their lives, / They should not reign as Tyrants o'er their wives. / Nor can the Women from this president / Insult, or triumph; it being aptly meant, / To teach both Sexes due equality; / And as they stand bound, to love mutually.

Its last two lines hold the whole formula: due equality, and mutual love between two people who are bound together. Neither victory nor surrender — equality between two people tied to each other. For Wen, Temperance is "the fusion of two contrasting elements and bringing them into harmony". And when the question is love in a relationship, the card, in her words, calls for "cooperation and tempering of extreme emotions, such as anger, resentment, hostility".

paragraphs.h3: The remedy Petruchio passed off as a trick

paragraphs: Shakespeare himself gave this couple a recipe for Temperance — through Petruchio's mouth, and as part of a trick. Throwing away the "burnt" meat, he says it is better for them to fast, "Since, of ourselves, ourselves are choleric". In the theory of temperament of the time, choler was the hot, angry humour, and two choleric people must not be given more fire. The trick becomes the truth once it is turned on oneself: when both are hot, anger is not fed — neither with food nor with words.

And at the wooing, Petruchio described Katherina with the very word of the main task: "She is not hot, but temperate as the morn". At the time it was a lie told to her father. The word spoken at the entry of the tail turned out to be the address the tail leads to.
If the links of this tail are put together the way Lisovskaya teaches one to connect the energies of a couple's tail, they come out like this:

ul: **The Lovers and Strength:** the common language of sparring easily becomes a struggle — flirting through challenge quietly turns into a score of jabs, and love starts being proved by winning.
**Strength and Temperance:** the main trap is who will out-stubborn whom; the way out is not to stop arguing but to stop adding fuel when both are hot.
**The Lovers and Temperance:** a love in which you were chosen rests on equality — giving way in turns, not by rank.
**All three cards:** a taming with no winner — every victory for one is recorded as a defeat for the couple.

sections.h2: The Lovers, Strength and Temperance in Waite: a chain of flowers and an angel without sex
paragraphs: The cards on this site have their own artwork. In the Rider–Waite–Smith deck, the three cards of this tail each add one detail to the story.

ul: **The Lovers.** A man and a woman beneath a winged figure, "unveiled before each other". The play begins the same way: from the first minute the two tell each other exactly what they think.

**Strength.** A woman closes a lion's jaws, and Waite stresses that the struggle is already over: "her beneficent fortitude has already subdued the lion, which is being led by a chain of flowers". The lion is not starved or kept awake — it is led on a chain of flowers. This is a direct answer to Shakespeare's falcon: a taming after which the beast stays a lion and walks alongside of its own accord. Petruchio wanted to turn a wildcat into a house cat; on Waite's Strength card the lion does not become a kitten.

**Temperance.** A winged figure pours "the essences of life from chalice to chalice", one foot on the earth and the other on the water. And one sentence of Waite's reads as if written for two plays about the war of the sexes: "I speak of him in the masculine sense, but the figure is neither male nor female." The angel of the main task is neither a man nor a woman.

paragraphs: Now it is clear why Maria's question about two drops is a question of Temperance: her card is water passing between two vessels. Wen quotes P. D. Ouspensky on this angel: "One of the cups the angel holds is the past, the other is the future. The rainbow stream between the cups is the present. You see that it flows both ways." The answer to Maria's question is that no drop is bound to run down first: the water goes back and forth. Even Katherina, in her final speech, compares an angry wife to a troubled fountain, "Muddy, ill-seeming, thick, bereft of beauty" — only she demands clear water from one side alone.

The plot of the two plays rests on the question of who tames whom — husband the wife or wife the husband. The main task of the tail removes the question: the figure of Temperance has no sex, so in this couple the role of tamer belongs to no one in particular. Measure is held by whoever can hold it at the moment.

sections.h2: The couple's values: a house, the world and an upside-down view
paragraphs: The couple's values are the point that shows what the union exists for. Couples with the 6-11-14 tail have one of three cards there: The Empress (47.9%), The World (29.1%) or The Hanged Man (23%). How they echo the plays is our own reading.

ul: **The Empress — a house in which something shared grows.** In Fletcher the house becomes a weapon: Maria demands that it be rebuilt and that a garden "of some twenty Acres" be laid out "of the Italian fashion", and every word from her husband about "due obedience", she says, "Shall cost you many a pound more". The value of The Empress is a house that two build together, not a fortress that one of them besieges.

**The World — acceptance without re-education.** In the minus of this card Lisovskaya sees remaking the partner to suit oneself — exactly Petruchio's programme. In the plus she sees full acceptance of the partner even at their worst, and no pressure at all. For these couples The World is a value that is the direct opposite of taming.

**The Hanged Man — the world upside down.** Katherina agrees to see the moon by day and a maiden in an old man, and in her agreement play can be heard for the first time, not defeat. Lisovskaya writes that couples with The Hanged Man often need a push from outside before they marry. Katherina's marriage really was pushed by other hands: her sister's suitors promised to pay Petruchio's wooing expenses, provided the elder sister was married off first. The value of The Hanged Man is the ability to look at the world through another person's eyes without losing one's own.

sections.h2: Example: the 6-11-14 tail for the couple 05.07.1975 and 05.07.1975
paragraphs: The site's engine gives the 6-11-14 tail to a couple whose two dates of birth are the same — 05.07.1975. This is the extreme case of the most "mirrored" combination: both partners have the personal tail 12-19-7 and the personal centre 5. The couple is the sum of two identical matrices:

Two Hanged Men make The Lovers, two Suns make Strength, two Chariots make Temperance. Each of the two, alone, is learning to drive their own chariot: 7 stands in the personal karmic task of both. Together the task is different — not to race each in their own chariot, but to blend. The middle is two Suns, the very "two raging fires" Petruchio spoke of before the wedding. Couples with identical personal tails 12-19-7 make up 22% of all couples with the 6-11-14 tail, and all of them have The Wheel of Fortune at the couple's centre: 5 + 5 = 10.

In this couple Temperance also stands at the point "What to create together": measure here is not only the task but also what the two met for. The Lovers recur at "What fills", "Path to prosperity" and "Where it leaks"; The Wheel stands both at the centre and at "Image of the couple"; at "Values" is The Empress. And the Judgement missing from the middle of the tail turns up at the point "Parents together".

sections.h2: How to live the 6-11-14 tail at its strongest
paragraphs: The tail predicts nothing. It shows where the same circle keeps repeating between two people, and what opens it.

ul: **Notice who names the sun.** If one partner always decides what counts as true, the atmosphere rests on the other's consent rather than on a game played by two.
**Tell sparring from war.** The common language of jabs is alive as long as tenderness can be heard in it. When only the score is left, it is time to change the conversation, not to win it.
**No taming by deprivation.** Not with food, sleep, money or silence. The Strength of this tail is the kind that leads, not the kind that keeps someone hungry.
**The rule of two drops.** Give way in turns, not by rank. If the same partner always yields first, it is no longer measure.
**When both are hot, add no fuel.** Putting a conversation off until morning is better than winning it at night.
**Write your own epilogue.** Agree that nobody has the right to reign and nobody may triumph over the one who lost.

paragraphs: The strong version of the 6-11-14 tail is a couple that has been through both plays and got stuck in neither. They still talk to each other in their own sharp language and still argue about where the sun is, but the argument has become a game against the world, not against each other. Whoever finds it easier at the moment gives way. They have no winner — not because their strength is equal, but because in this tail one partner's victory is always a defeat for both.

intro: That is the hidden plot of this tail. Two people are drawn together by a wish for love without masks; their road runs through a contest over who will tame whom; and their main task is to blend two hot tempers so that neither a tamer nor a tamed one is left in the couple.

ul: **6 · The Lovers — entry to the task.** What the two want together: a love where each can be themselves and where each was chosen. From the first meeting they share a common language — the language of sparring. It also becomes their first resistance.
**11 · Strength — middle of the task.** What the couple goes through: a trial of strength, a fight for the last word, and the discovery that you can only tame someone who has agreed to it.

**14 · Temperance — main task.** What to learn: measure. Not letting the same person give way every time, not adding fuel when both are hot, and seeing that here one partner's victory is always a defeat for both.

intro: Four hundred years ago this plot was played out in two plays about one and the same husband. In Shakespeare's The Taming of the Shrew, Petruchio tames Katherina. In the sequel written by John Fletcher, the same Petruchio marries again — and this time he is the one being tamed. Together the two plays walk the 6-11-14 tail from start to finish, and Fletcher put the answer to its main task into his epilogue.

faq.q: How is the 6-11-14 couple tail different from a personal karmic tail?
faq.a: There is no personal 6-11-14 tail: for one person the middle of the tail is the reduced sum of the entry and the main task, and with an entry of 6 and a task of 14 it is always 20, Judgement. In a couple each point is the sum of the same points of two personal matrices, so Strength ends up in the middle. The roles of the points differ too: entry to the task, middle of the task and the couple's main task, not one person's karma.

faq.q: Are there couple tails with the same numbers in a different order?
faq.a: No. Among the 97 couple tails these three numbers occur only in the order 6-11-14. The order matters: the entry to the task always comes first and the main task last.

faq.q: Does the 6-11-14 tail mean that one partner will dominate the other?
faq.a: No. The tail describes a theme the two go through, not an outcome. Strength in the middle speaks of a trial of strength, and the main task, Temperance, of leaving it with no winner. The roles of tamer and tamed are tied neither to sex nor to character, and in a real couple they often swap.

faq.q: How common is the 6-11-14 karmic tail in compatibility?
faq.a: Roughly one couple in 25 has it — 3.95% of couples; it is the fourth most common of the 97 couple tails. It is made up of five combinations of personal tails, most often 15-20-5 and 18-9-9 (45% of such couples), 15-5-8 and 18-6-6 (30%), and two identical 12-19-7 tails (22%).

faq.q: Why does the couple have The Sun at the centre if one person never does?
faq.a: The couple's centre is the sum of two personal centres. For one person 19 never falls at the centre, whatever the date, but for two it adds up from 9 and 10, from 7 and 12 or, more rarely, from 5 and 14. So The Sun at the centre of these couples is an atmosphere that neither of the two brought along: they can only create it together.

report: The middle of the 6-11-14 tail holds a card that could never stand there for a single person. One person alone always travels from The Lovers to Temperance through Judgement: 6 + 14 = 20. In a couple the middle is added up by two, and in the place of Judgement stands Strength. No verdict comes from outside — the two are left alone with each other, and they start taming each other.

Four hundred years ago this plot was played out in two plays about one and the same husband. In Shakespeare's The Taming of the Shrew, Petruchio tames Katherina. In John Fletcher's sequel, The Tamer Tamed, the same Petruchio marries again — and this time he is the one being tamed. Together the plays walk the tail in order: the wooing is The Lovers, taming in both directions is Strength, the epilogue is Temperance.

report.h3: A sting hidden in the tail

report: A couple with this tail is drawn together by a wish for a love in which each can be themselves, and its common language appears with the very first line — the language of sparring. A minute after meeting, Katherina and Petruchio are finishing each other's puns: "— Who knows not where a wasp does wear his sting? In his tail. — In his tongue." Petruchio is the first to answer her at her own speed. With him there is no need to pretend.

But the same wish turns into resistance at once. Katherina's shrewishness grows from the fact that her sister is loved and she is not. Her father tells the suitor that her love is the main thing, "all in all"; Petruchio replies, "Why, that is nothing" — and marries her willing or not. Others think such a pair is quarrelling; the two think they are talking. The trouble starts when tenderness can no longer be heard in the language of jabs and only the score is left.

Petruchio promises to turn a "wild Kate" into a "household" one — Kate sounds like cat — and tames her as a falconer tames a hawk: with hunger and sleeplessness, all of it "in reverend care of her". The servants sum it up: "He kills her in her own humour" — "he is more shrew than she". He had warned of it himself: "where two raging fires meet together / They do consume the thing that feeds their fury". **The first trap of Strength in a couple is competing over who can hold out longer.** Pressure here rarely looks like an order; more often it looks like care that leaves the other no choice. If one partner holds the other through fear, by withholding food, sleep or money, or through threats, this is no longer the task of the tail but a boundary: outside help is needed — a psychologist, a crisis line, and in danger, a local emergency number.

Fletcher saw what Shakespeare had left offstage. The late Katherina, friends recall, "turn'd his temper" and forced Petruchio to storm as high as she did; he calls that taming twelve labours that would have driven even Hercules mad. His second wife, Maria, declares, "I am no more the gentle, tame Maria" — and turns his own means against him: refusal, siege, a bet on endurance. One and the same man was both the tamer and the tamed. **The role in the middle of this tail is tied neither to sex nor to character** — it passes from hand to hand.

When honest Strength runs short, the two stage a Judgement. In Fletcher, Petruchio pretends to be dead, Maria pronounces a verdict over the coffin on his "foolish life", and he rises and says, "I am born again." In a comedy it works. In a couple such a scene brings relief but not measure: only the winner has changed.

The most famous scene of The Taming of the Shrew is an argument on the road. It is broad day, Petruchio insists it is the moon, and he orders the horses turned back. Katherina answers that whatever he chooses to name it, "even that it is; / And so it shall be so for Katharina." It can be heard as surrender: one decides what counts as the sun, the other agrees. Or it can be heard as the start of a game. A minute later Petruchio greets an old man as a fair young maid, and Katherina joins in so warmly that the old man calls her his merry mistress. For the first time the two laugh not at each other but together. Right after this Petruchio asks for a kiss in the middle of the street, and she kisses him, calling him "love" for the first time. The entry of the tail is fulfilled not at the altar but here.

The main task is Temperance, and both plays end in its minus: one gives way, the other never thinks of it. In her final speech Katherina tells the wives to lower their pride, so measure is demanded of one side only; the last line of the play has its doubts: it is a wonder, it says, that she lets herself be tamed so. Maria, having won, at once vows to be her husband's servant. The score has flipped, but it has not disappeared.

Fletcher had put the answer into Maria's mouth earlier: "Take two small drops of water, equal weigh'd, / Tell me which is the heaviest, and which ought / First to descend in duty?" The question of Temperance is not who is right but who gives way. The epilogue answers: the play is meant "To teach both Sexes due equality; / And as they stand bound, to love mutually." In Waite, the figure of Temperance pours water from chalice to chalice and, in his words, is "neither male nor female"; and the lion of his Strength is led on a chain of flowers, with nobody starving it.

There is also a Shakespearean recipe passed off as a trick. Throwing away the "burnt" meat, Petruchio explains that such food is not for them, "Since, of ourselves, ourselves are choleric". **When both are hot, anger is not fed — neither with food nor with words.** And at the wooing he lied to her father that Katherina was "not hot, but temperate as the morn". The word spoken at the entry turned out to be the address the tail leads to.

The strong version of the 6-11-14 tail is a couple that has been through both plays and got stuck in neither. The two still talk in their own sharp language and still argue about where the sun is, but the argument has become a game against the world, not against each other. Whoever finds it easier at the moment gives way. **They have no winner: in this tail one partner's victory is always a defeat for both.**

unit.meaning: Your couple goes through a contest over who tames whom, and wins only when that contest leaves no winner.
